title: Subhuti asks (section 2)
hook: how should one set out on the bodhisattva path, and hold the mind?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diamond Sutra opened on an ordinary morning: robe, bowl, alms, a meal, washed feet, a seat. Your line: an ordinary morning. Which chore did you do all the way through? Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

The Buddha has just sat down. The monks have settled around him. The grove is quiet. Somebody has to go first. Classrooms know this moment: the teacher is ready, the room is full, and nobody wants to be the one to break the silence with a question that might sound foolish. In the Diamond Sutra, one monk stands up. He's an elder, and his name is Subhuti. What he asks is the question the whole sutra will spend itself answering. Today: Subhuti asks.
screen: `THE ROOM IS QUIET.` → `SOMEBODY HAS TO GO FIRST.` → `ONE MONK STANDS.`

segments.voice: First, how he asks. The sutra slows down to show it. Subhuti rises from his place in the assembly. He arranges his upper robe over one shoulder, kneels on his right knee, joins his palms toward the Buddha, and bows. The body asks before the mouth does. Second, what he says first. Not his question. He begins with wonder: how much the bodhisattvas have been helped, he says, how much they've been cared for by the Tathagata. Before he asks for anything, he notices what's already been given. Third, the question itself. Paraphrased: when someone has set out on the bodhisattva path, how should they stand? How should they go on? And how should they hold the mind? Three parts, really one. Where do I put my feet, how do I keep walking, and what do I do with this restless thing behind my eyes? It's a beginner's question, and Subhuti is no beginner. That's part of its force. The elder asks it on behalf of everyone who's just starting. Fourth, the answer that isn't one yet. The Buddha says, well said, Subhuti, well said. Listen, and take it well to heart, and I'll tell you. And Subhuti says, so be it, and waits. That's the whole of section two. The question is asked, praised, and left hanging in the air overnight. Some readers find that a teaching too. A good question deserves a moment of silence before anyone rushes to answer it. From tomorrow, the answers start coming, and they take a sharp turn.
screen: `THE BODY ASKS FIRST.` · `WONDER BEFORE THE QUESTION.` · `HOW TO STAND, GO, HOLD THE MIND.` · `WELL SAID. LISTEN.` · then, large: `HOW TO HOLD THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: ask your own central question. Settle, and breathe. Sit up a little, the way Subhuti knelt, with some care in how you hold yourself. Then ask: what is the question under my questions right now? Not the to-do list. The one underneath. How do I love this person well? What am I for? How do I hold my mind when it races? Let it come in your own words. Don't answer it. Just ask it once, clearly, and let it hang in the quiet, the way his did. The bell holds the time.
Subhuti. The elder monk who rises, kneels, and asks the Diamond Sutra's question: how to stand, how to go on, how to hold the mind. Today's word.

Your line: how to hold the mind. Today, when your mind runs off, ask Subhuti's question once, quietly, and notice what the asking does. Tomorrow, all beings freed, none freed. Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: In monasteries that follow this custom, a monk who asks a teacher a question in assembly rises, arranges the robe over one shoulder, kneels and joins palms, as Subhuti does in the Diamond Sutra; the sutra itself is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the name of the elder who questions the Buddha in the Diamond Sutra.

trapdoor: what you thought: Subhuti is a student with a beginner's question.
what it means: he's an elder who asks on behalf of everyone starting out: how to stand, go on, and hold the mind.
what a scholar hears: section 2 is the sutra's frame question; the Buddha's 'well said, listen' delays the answer to section 3.
